$comment: Copy to <repo>/.claude/review-policy.json and EDIT FOR THAT REPO, then commit it.
It decides which AI reviewers a PR must pass, so it is a reviewed artefact: change it in a PR, never ad hoc.
Rules: any file matching 'high' => HIGH. Every file matching 'low' => LOW. Anything else => NORMAL.
Omitting the file entirely is safe and means everything is NORMAL.
'low' is the dangerous list. A path belongs there only if it is provably unreachable from
every deploy path IN THIS REPO - which is repo-specific fact a generic hook cannot know.
Worked example: a .dockerignore is LOW in a repo whose frontend ships via npm +
static-web-apps-deploy and whose CI only pulls a postgres service container, because no
deployed artefact is built from a Dockerfile. In a repo that ships a container image, the
same file is NORMAL. Do not copy this list between repos without re-checking that.
The first two high entries are the REVIEW CONTROL PLANE and must stay HIGH in every
repo. This file decides which reviewers a PR needs, and .coderabbit.yaml can silence a
reviewer outright. Left unlisted they classify as NORMAL - so the one edit that can
disable review everywhere would itself get the lighter review.
.gitignore USED to be the third, because re-excluding .claude/ makes this file vanish
and a repo with no policy tiers every PR NORMAL. It was removed 2026-08-02: tiering is
path-glob only, so it could not distinguish that edit from ignoring a scratch directory,
and every trivial ignore change billed a scarce CodeRabbit review. The invariant is now
asserted directly in CI instead - a step that fails if .claude/review-policy.json is
untracked or ignored (git ls-files --error-unmatch, plus git check-ignore --no-index;
--no-index is load-bearing, as check-ignore never reports a TRACKED file as ignored).
That is deterministic and free where a reviewer noticing was neither. Do NOT re-add
.gitignore here without first checking whether that CI guard is present in the repo.
DEPENDENCY MANIFESTS ARE DELIBERATELY ABSENT from 'high' (package.json, package-lock.json,
Directory.Packages.props, **/*.csproj). They are what Dependabot edits, and dependency PRs
are out of AI code review on both vendors: CodeRabbit refuses bot authors outright
('Review skipped: bot user not eligible for review'), and Gitar's bot review is switched
off on purpose because reviewing every bump would exhaust both budgets. Listing them HIGH
would demand a reviewer that can never run - coverage on paper, none in fact. CI plus
Dependabot's own advisory data is what gates them. Add them back only if that changes.
'.github/workflows/**' LEFT the high list on 2026-08-19, for the same reason .gitignore did,
and is asserted in review-policy-guard.yml instead. Measured across 100 HIGH PRs in the
preceding 30 days: config-only diffs were 27 of them and produced FOUR actionable CodeRabbit
comments in total, while code-bearing diffs produced 174. In that same sample 45 of 100 HIGH
PRs received NO CodeRabbit verdict at all - throttled out, CodeRabbit's own notice reporting
73 reviews in 7 days against a 30/7d degradation threshold. The glob was therefore not buying
review of workflow changes; it was crowding out review of code, and which PRs got reviewed
was decided by arrival time rather than by risk.
What a reviewer was nominally catching on a workflow diff is now checked mechanically:
unpinned actions, pull_request_target, and a blanket write-all token, plus actionlint in CI.
Deleting the guard is covered by branch rules, not review - 'Review policy intact' is a
REQUIRED status check, so removing the workflow means the check never reports and the PR
cannot merge. Do NOT re-add '.github/workflows/**' here without first removing those
assertions from the guard.
THE MERGE BARRIER ITSELF IS HIGH, added 2026-08-23 after an adversarial-review sweep found
the same hole in six estate repos at once. 'CI Gate' is a REQUIRED status check, but it is
produced by the PR's own copy of ci.yml - so a PR that keeps the job, its name and its needs:
list, and only guts the aggregation step, reports green while gating nothing. Same for the
checker that asserts the wiring, and for the guard workflow that asserts this file. All three
were tiering NORMAL while protecting the merge barrier, which is the lightest review the
highest-leverage edit in the repo could possibly get.
Note what this is NOT: it is three named paths, not a re-added '.github/workflows/**' glob.
The glob was removed because it billed a scarce review for every routine workflow edit; these
three files change a few times a year, and assert_gate_coverage.py now checks the gate's own
semantics mechanically (if: always(), a step keyed on needs.<job>.result, no conditional job
feeding the gate). Review is the backstop for the edits a checker cannot see - like deleting
the check step itself. Adjust the ci.yml path if this repo's main workflow is named
differently; a HIGH entry pointing at a file that does not exist protects nothing.
'.github/dependabot.yml' DOES stay HIGH. It is edited a few times a year, so it costs almost
nothing, and a change to it alters what gets patched and how fast - which is not something
the guard's assertions can see.
Registry/feed and analyzer-enforcement config DOES stay HIGH (nuget.config, global.json,
.config/dotnet-tools.json, .npmrc, Directory.Build.props). A bot does not edit these; a human repointing a package
feed or relaxing TreatWarningsAsErrors does, and that is a supply-chain or
enforcement change a reviewer should see. Note NuGet.config is listed twice for casing:
globs compile to case-SENSITIVE regexes, and both spellings occur in the wild.
ANY SCRIPT A GATED JOB RUNS BELONGS HERE, and you do not have to remember to add it:
assert_gate_coverage.py DERIVES that requirement from what ci.yml actually invokes and
fails when a merge-blocking job runs a repo-local script no high glob covers. So when this
repo grows its own checker - a coverage floor, a release gate, a deploy assertion - add its
path here (or cover the directory with a glob such as 'scripts/**') and the derived check
passes. It runs from the PR's OWN checkout, so an edit changing its failure path to exit 0
would otherwise merge a neutered gate green under the lighter review. Enumeration alone had
already failed twice in one estate repo before the check was derived instead.
